2    Q.   WOULD YOU PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND ADDRESS?

3    A.   My name is Doug Gegax. My address is 4805 Sage Road, Las Cruces, New Mexico, 88011.

4    Q.   WHERE ARE YOU EMPLOYED?

5    A.   I am currently a Professor Emeritus at New Mexico State University (“NMSU”). I retired from

6         NMSU on January 1, 2022 where I had been employed since 1984. Prior to my retirement, I

7         was a Distinguished Achievement Professor in the Department of Economics and Applied

8         Statistics as well as the Director of the Center for Public Utilities (“CPU”) in the College of

9         Business at NMSU. For the purposes of this proceeding, I am engaged through Doug Gegax

10        Consulting, a New Mexico-registered consulting firm. The expert opinions expressed herein

11        are my own and nothing in this testimony necessarily reflects the opinions of NMSU or the

12        CPU. I am testifying on behalf of the New Mexico Department of Justice (“NMDOJ”).

13   Q.   WOULD YOU PLEASE DESCRIBE YOUR EDUCATIONAL AND PROFESSIONAL

14        QUALIFICATIONS?

15   A.   I have been engaged in public utility regulation for over forty years. I received a Ph.D. in

16        Economics from The University of Wyoming in 1985, specializing in Utility Regulation, Public

17        Finance, Econometrics, and Environmental Economics. As a consultant, I have served a variety

18        of clients including regulatory agencies, utility customers, utility companies, the U.S.

19        Department of Energy, and the U.S. Department of Justice. I have actively served as a

20        consultant for the NMDOJ/Attorney General since 1999. I have previously filed written

21        testimony or helped prepare rates-related filings in the following jurisdictions: Arizona,

22        Arkansas, Colorado, Hawaii, Nevada, New Mexico, and the Federal Energy Regulatory

23        Commission. I have given oral testimony in front of the New Mexico Public Regulation

11   Q.         WHAT IS THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN CUSTOMER-RELATED COSTS AND

12              DEMAND-RELATED COSTS?

13   A.         In a class cost-of-service study, costs that do not vary with kWh usage are typically deemed to

14              be “fixed costs.” These fixed costs are comprised of customer-related costs as well as demand-

15              related costs (also known as capacity-related costs). Customer-related costs are sensitive to

16              adding customers to the system and do not change with customer kWh usage or kW loads put

17              on the system. Examples of customer-related costs are costs associated with service drops,

18              meters, meter reading and installation, customer billing, maintaining customer records,

19              customer-related A&G, and other customer-related services. Demand-related costs are sensitive

20              to the demands (loads) placed on the system, which affect the amount of capacity required to

21              satisfy these loads.       While both are considered fixed costs, the key distinction between

22              customer-related costs and demand-related costs is that demand-related costs are sensitive to

2    Q.      PLEASE PROVIDE AN OVERVIEW OF SPS’S PROPOSED EAP?

3    A.      As described on page 101 of Zoe E. Lees direct testimony and pages 41 – 48 of Taylor J. Hurt’s

4            direct testimony, SPS’s proposed EAP would provide supplemental customer assistance to

5            households with low-incomes and high energy burdens25. The EAP would cover a portion of

6            the customers’ electricity bills in either the four summer months (June, July, August and

7            September) or the four winter months (November, December, January and February). SPS’s

8            proposed EAP would be available to New Mexico SPS retail Residential customers who are

9            qualified for – and receive assistance from – the New Mexico Low-Income Home Energy

10           Assistance Program (“LIHEAP”), which distributes federal funds to low-income households.

11           SPS does not seek to make an independent determination of a customer’s income eligibility;

12           rather, SPS proposes to make EAP benefits available to its residential customers who have

13           already established eligibility under LIHEAP.

14   Q.      HOW DOES SPS PROPOSE TO FUND THE EAP?

15   A.      SPS proposes an initially conservative EAP program budget of $750,000, which will be funded

16           through a rider that is in addition to the cost of providing electric service. Funding for the EAP

17           will be obtained from all customer classes – both residential and non-residential – through a flat

18           EAP charge on their bill. The amount of the annual budget allocated to each customer class is

19           based a 25% weighting of the class’s cost of service portion of the total cost of service and a

20           75% weighting of the class’s customer count portion of the total customer count. The EAP rider
